The Hiring Huddle: Job Seeker Edition 

Only 29,000 jobs were added in September. If you're job hunting, is your search built for this market?

The Labor Department's September report came in far below the roughly 85,000 to 90,000 economists expected. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2%. The prior month's gain was also revised down, from 162K to 133K.

The market hasn't collapsed, but it has cooled. For anyone looking, that changes the game plan.

What's working:
• Referrals and warm intros. When postings get crowded, a name inside the building matters more.
• A resume that mirrors the job description's language, with numbers on results.
• Specialized skills tied to a business problem, like security, data, and AI.
• Contract and project roles as a way in. Companies that won't commit to a full-time headcount will often still bring in a consultant.

What's not:
• Mass-applying to 100 jobs. Volume without targeting just feeds the pile.
• Waiting for the "perfect" posting.
• A generic LinkedIn headline.

My advice is to pick 10 target companies, work two warm connections at each, and follow up like it's your job. In football terms, you're running a ball-control offense now, not throwing deep on every down.

The Python conversation in 2026 is dominated by free-threading performance and AI-driven code generation, but the most strategic shift I am tracking is the quiet adoption of type-driven design as a first-class architectural discipline, not just a linting nicety.

I have been working with teams that have fully embraced Python's type system as the primary mechanism for defining their domain boundaries and enforcing invariants. The obvious story is that type hints make code more readable and catch obvious errors. The non-obvious lesson is what happens to your system's resilience when every function signature becomes a contract that the runtime can validate, and when your type checker becomes the first line of defense against entire categories of business logic bugs. Teams adopting this pattern are reporting a 50% reduction in production incidents caused by incorrect data shapes flowing between services, because the type system catches the mismatch at the integration point, not at the point of failure. The most expensive failure in modern Python systems is not a slow query -- it is a silent data corruption that propagates through three services before anyone notices.

The second under-discussed development is the maturation of "protocol-based polymorphism" as the default pattern for building testable, swappable components. The overlooked insight is not the ability to write abstract base classes but the ability to define structural subtyping that lets you mock entire subsystems without touching a single class hierarchy. I have seen teams eliminate entire classes of integration test regressions because they can now define a protocol for a database adapter and swap in a test double that satisfies the same interface without inheritance. The system reasons about behavior through contracts, not through inheritance trees.

For hiring managers and talent acquisition specialists: the candidate who can explain why their Python strategy treats the type system as a design tool for defining domain boundaries and preventing data corruption, and why they use protocols over inheritance for testability, is the one who will protect your organization from the most expensive failure modes: the silent data corruption that cascades through your architecture and the test suite that requires a full integration environment to validate component boundaries. The engineer who understands that modern Python is about building systems where correctness is proven at the type-checking layer, not the runtime, will design platforms that are both expressive and provably safe.

Many companies are talking about AI transformation this year. But in many cases teams are discovering the hard way: handing an LLM to an engineering team can not only accelerate shipping, and sometimes it will also accelerate technical debt. The result is a codebase with a lot of duplicates, strange technical decisions that are hard to understand, and hard-to-fix issues in production. AI-driven software engineering is more about communicating and cooperating with AI instead of writing the code.

Here are several examples that must be covered by an AI transformation:

- Engineers must own the code and understand the context. If the project is huge, it won’t be in the AI context fully. AI doesn’t know the critical details about workflows, pipelines, and ideas inside of your project. If you ask an AI model to build a feature without deep context about your project, it will hallucinate architecture, reinvent existing utilities, and write a lot of boilerplate. An engineer must cover these situations. Using a weak prompt will produce an unpredictable generation: "Add a function that creates a payment object and fills it with user’s data." Possible result - the model reinvents models, guesses contracts, and duplicates logic. Much better would be to add context to that prompt and explain the engineers’ requirements: "Create a function to add a new payment using methods from our PaymentProcessor class. It should return a filled Payment object. Input must be a Client and amount; currency is optional with USD as the default." With this prompt the model returns a predictable result with less hallucinations. In most cases AI doesnt know full architecture unless you feed it clear constraints, existing classes, and strict expectations.

- Test-First (TDD) is a must with AI-assisted engineering. An AI can generate 200 lines of code, and an engineer can miss an edge case during the review. The result is these bugs reach production servers. To avoid this, just go with these steps: define the specifications, write the unit tests/integration tests before writing the code, ask AI to verify if all edge cases are covered, and only after this you can ask AI to write the code. The final step: manual audit and verifying if AI produced exactly the same code as you needed. Because even with excellent tests AI can hallucinate and write the code that passes the tests, but doesn’t do the desired things.

- Not every engineer wants this transformation. Some resist using AI tools, while others accept the results too uncritically. Tools dont automatically make an engineering organization faster, better, and cleaner. Finding engineers who combine deep foundational software and architecture design with significant responsibility while working with AI is a tricky thing.

IT Recruitment in 2026: Real Gains, Thin Evidence

IT recruitment in 2026 has improved in real ways, but the claim that it is getting better for everyone rests on weaker evidence than the headlines suggest.

The gains are genuine. Bullhorn's 2026 survey of nearly 2,300 job seekers found that 81% of those who met AI through their agency rated it positively, and 93% of those with a good experience would use that agency again. Scheduling, screening and out-of-hours replies suit machines, leaving recruiters time for judgement and relationships.

Skills-based hiring is spreading too. Michael Page reports that more than eight in ten UK tech organisations practise it, against 66% nationally, citing fairness, better matching and clearer insight into capability. Robert Half's research shows employers pairing permanent and contract hires with upskilling, a pragmatic answer to scarce AI, cloud and cybersecurity talent.

Now the challenge. Nearly all this evidence comes from recruiters and software vendors with a commercial interest, and it measures sentiment and intent, not outcomes. The 93% figure covers only candidates who already had a good experience, saying nothing about those screened out who never heard back. The skills figure shows what employers say they do, not who actually gets hired. The Robert Half numbers describe expectations, not results.

The gains are also uneven. Addison Group describes modest growth, budget freezes and demand concentrated in cloud, data, AI and cybersecurity, with salaries projected to rise 8-10%, slower than before. The winners hold scarce, current skills. For juniors and career changers the picture is unclear. Better skills assessment doesn't create more willing candidates either: 59% of tech hiring managers still see scarce talent as a major barrier.

So the defensible position is cautious optimism, tested on outcomes rather than sentiment. Teams can check their own data:

- Time from application to offer, before and after AI tools
- Satisfaction and drop-off for all applicants, including rejected ones
- Pass-through rates at each stage, by group
- Share of hires without a degree, year on year
- Offer acceptance and 90-day retention
- How many applicants get a reply, and how fast

If those numbers improve, the case is made. Candidates should expect skills assessments and ask how AI is used in screening. Until the outcome data arrives, 2026's recruitment story is promising, but still mostly a story?

Staffing Trends 2026: Where India and the Middle East Are Hiring

Where is white-collar and IT hiring actually growing?
Here's the latest domain-by-domain view for India and the Middle East.

Growing:
- AI/ML: +20%, the clear leader
- Auto: +11%
- BPO/ITES: +4%
- GCCs: +4%
Stable: BFSI, insurance, retail, real estate
Slowing:
- IT/software services: -4%
- Pharma/biotech: -4%
- FMCG: -4%
- Healthcare: -3%

By experience: demand is rising for 8–16 years (+5% to +7%), while 4–7 years dipped 2%. Clients want people who can own outcomes, not just tasks.
By city: Hyderabad (+9%), Chennai (+6%) and Bengaluru (+4%) are leading. Delhi-NCR and Mumbai are down 6% each.

MIDDLE EAST
- IT & Telecom: +30% across the Gulf (UAE +32%, KSA +13%)
- Software & hardware roles in the UAE: +46%
- Retail, trade & logistics: +16%
- Oil & gas (-8%) and petrochemicals (-9%) are cooling
- Oman (+11%) and Qatar (+9%) are the fastest-growing hiring markets right now
- The drivers are data centres, cloud and AI-ready infrastructure, with engineers, developers and infrastructure specialists most in demand.

What this means for staffing:
1. Demand is shifting from IT services to GCCs and end clients. Candidates need end-to-end ownership, not module-level experience.
2. AI/ML, cloud, cybersecurity and data are where the volume and premiums are.
3. Senior and mid-senior professionals are in short supply. Speed to offer decides who wins the candidate.
4. In the Gulf, IT demand is broad-based, not just oil and gas. Smaller markets like Oman and Qatar are opening up.
5. BFSI and insurance remain a steady base for contract staffing in both regions.

DPDP is coming for our hiring process. Is the system ready?

DPDP does not stop us from hiring or verifying candidates. It stops careless data handling. A strong ATS in recruitment is a basic need, not a nice-to-have.

What will get scrutinized
•	Resumes, interview notes and ATS records held with no clear reason or end date.
•	Background checks that collect more than the role needs.
•	Agencies and vendors handling candidate data with no proper contract.
•	Weak security. The Act allows penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to protect personal data.

What is still safe
•	Asking for data that is needed for the role
•	Verifying degrees, past employers and identity, with clear communication

What candidates should be told
•	What Data we collect and why.
•	Which vendors or agencies will see it.
•	How long we keep it, and how they can ask for correction or deletion.
•	Where AI or automation is used in screening.

What should stop
•	"Collect everything just in case" checks on finance, health or criminal history for roles that do not need them.
•	Vague forms such as "any issues in the past?"
•	Resumes forwarded on WhatsApp or personal email.
•	Keeping rejected candidates' data forever.

Are there loopholes? Well... Yes! And until it's all clear, take notice and consent where in doubt. The content of the consent form needs to be elaborate and explicit.

We have about seven months. A good candidate experience now includes respect for candidate data.

Which part of your hiring process would you find hardest to defend today?

Closing the trust gap in your hiring process

This months client newsletter from @Aspire jobs delves into the CV-Library Candidate Behaviour Barometer 2026 which surveyed 1,043 candidates and 233 recruiters and employers in August. 

Its central finding is a trust gap: both sides look at the same hiring process and see something different, and several of those differences are costing businesses good hires.Within our newsletter Aspire Jobs give our top tips for each of these sections.... 

➡️Your application process - Some 96% of recruiters rate their application process as streamlined or fairly efficient, yet 71% of candidates have abandoned an application because it was too long or complicated. That figure reaches 81% among IT candidates

➡️ Speed - Eight in ten candidates expect a decision within seven days of interview, but only a third of employers complete hiring within two weeks, and for direct employers the figure is 25%. Our own average time to fill, from taking the role to securing an offer, was 25.5 dayslast quarter (UK average is 40-42 days)

➡️Salary and reputation - Around 95% of candidates want salary information in the advert, and 41% say a missing salary could stop them applying. A poor company reputation is the biggest deal-breaker at 47%, and 35% are put off by negative online reviews.

➡️Accepted offers - Over half of candidates (52%) would accept an offer and keep looking, up from 24% last year, and 48% do not trust an offer until the contract is signed and they have started work.

➡️AI applicationsome 69% of recruiters say AI-generated applications make strong candidates harder to identify. We screen every CV by hand, and we can tell when AI has written one, which takes longer but shows us who is genuinely suited to your role. We also respond to almost every applicant and pass on whatever interview feedback we receive.

If any of this sounds familiar, give me a call. Most of these fixes cost nothing and can be in place quickly, and I am happy to look through your process with you and tell you honestly where candidates are likely to be dropping out. Contact me helen@aspirejobs.co.uk.

A completed contract is not a failed commitment.

Yet somehow, in 2026, we're still treating project-based careers as a red flag.

I've had a few conversations with recruiters recently, and the same questions keep coming up:

"Why haven't you stayed at one company for 10 years?"

"Why have you worked with so many different organizations?"

Here's the thing: Not every career is built around permanent employment.

Much of my experience has been in consulting, fixed-term contracts, and project-based engagements across gaming, esports, commercial partnerships, marketing, and live events.

You join with a defined objective. You take ownership. You deliver. Sometimes the assignment ends, and you move on.

That's not necessarily job-hopping. That's how project-based work operates, i fucking hated sometimes absolutely but it puts food on the table.

I value autonomy, accountability, transparency, and straightforward communication. I want to work with people who care more about what gets delivered than how long someone has occupied the same desk.

And while LinkedIn is full of success stories, here's a less glamorous reality:

I've been looking for my next opportunity for a while. Recently, I signed a contract with a Saudi-based company. Two days later, they backed out, citing budget issues.

Two days. After signing. 

No motivational spin here. It's frustrating, and the market can be brutal.

But I'm still here, still building relationships, and still looking for the right opportunity.

I'm not looking for a company where I can simply collect years of tenure. I'm looking for one where I can contribute, challenge ideas constructively, take ownership, and create measurable value.

A question for hiring managers: When did tenure become a more important measure of someone's value than what they've actually delivered?

And to companies hiring in gaming, esports, partnerships, sponsorships, or commercial growth: I'm open to a meaningful conversation.💪🏽

6 days from a 30-minute briefing to an accepted offer.

My most recent recruitment assignment started on 30 September. There was no polished job description waiting for me. The client came to me with the role, the technical stack, and an idea of the person they needed. 
So we started with a 30-minute conversation. We covered the technical requirements, seniority, personality and team fit, salary budget, working model and, importantly, when they actually wanted this person to start. From there, I built the recruitment process.

This was my funnel: 
Role briefing → Job specification → Market mapping → Sourcing → Outreach → Screening → Shortlist → Client interviews → Verba Offer →Contract signed 

And this is where I think recruitment today becomes really interesting, because the process was a combination of technology, AI, automation, and human judgement.
I used Claude to help structure and refine the job description. I posted the role on my favourite job board, JustJoinIT, and yes, as always, I negotiated a good commercial deal with the consultant there. 
😉I used LinkedIn Recruiter and X-Ray searches to map the market and build the initial pipeline. Then I used Juicebox to expand the search and support candidate outreach.

But technology was only part of it. Behind those tools was a lot of searching, reviewing profiles, adjusting the search, understanding who was actually relevant and speaking to people. 

The numbers looked like this:
~800 profiles reached/identified
↓~300 candidates actively approached or reviewed through direct search and applications
↓12 screening conversations
↓4 candidates introduced to the client
↓2 invited to face-to-face interviews
↓1 offer
↓1 hire

The right candidate had their face-to-face interview on 5 October. The offer was made on 7 October. Time to hire: 10 days. And I’m particularly happy about this one because my historically short time-to-hire hasn’t disappeared as the tools around recruitment have changed. 

If anything, the tools make me faster. But they don’t decide which four people I should put in front of a hiring manager. They don’t understand the conversation behind a brief that doesn’t even have a job description yet. And they don’t build trust with a candidate who wasn’t necessarily planning to change jobs. That’s where the recruiter still matters. And this assignment was a great reminder of how much I enjoy working closely with clients, understanding what they really need, and helping them grow their teams quickly and effectively

YOUR NEXT CAREER OPPORTUNITY MAY BE IN A COUNTRY YOU'VE NEVER CONSIDERED.

We often search for jobs within familiar borders. But what if the geography of your search is limiting your opportunities?

According to Eurostat, unemployment across the EU stood at 6.1% in August 2026. Yet the differences between countries are significant:

→ Finland — 10.3%
→ Spain — 10.0%
→ Estonia — 8.0%
→ Germany — 4.0%
→ Poland — 3.4%
→ Czechia — 3.2%

These numbers don't tell us where the best jobs are. But they reveal something important: Europe is not one uniform labour market.

For professionals whose work can be delivered digitally — designers, developers, marketers, content creators and AI specialists — this raises an interesting question:

Why limit your job search to one country?

A broader international search can help you:

→ Discover companies and industries outside your local market.
→ Explore opportunities in economies with different hiring conditions.
→ Connect directly with international employers and decision-makers.
→ Consider remote employment, freelance contracts and project-based collaboration.

Of course, a low unemployment rate doesn't automatically mean more vacancies. And not every remote position allows cross-border employment.

Industry demand, language requirements, hiring regulations and the employer's remote-work policy matter just as much.

The goal isn't to chase the country with the lowest unemployment rate. It's to stop treating your local job market as the limit of your professional opportunities.

🎬 Two judgments in two days, one national enforcement law and a VLOP designation ruling due on 14 October: a new episode of 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁(𝘀) 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 is out.

🇮🇹 Italy names its AI Act enforcers
Law No. 177 sets out which authorities will enforce the AI Act in Italy. Market surveillance authorities and financial oversight institutions, including the Bank of Italy and the financial markets supervisor, are called to assess the declared risks of high-risk AI systems, while data protection authorities are kept in the loop and participate within the limits of their mandate. The law also bans fully automated HR decisions on hiring, dismissal, disciplinary measures and performance reviews. A complex mechanism that will only work if those authorities cooperate in practice.

📄 Zalando v Commission (T-203/24)
On 7 October 2026, the General Court dismissed Zalando’s challenge to the Commission’s refusal to disclose the documents used to calculate its DSA supervisory fee, holding that the Commission lawfully relied on the protection of third-party commercial interests and ongoing judicial proceedings. The judgment marks the limits of transparency around the methodologies and datasets behind VLOP supervision.

📞 Digi România and Investcapital (C-872/24 and C-909/24)
On 8 October 2026, the Court confirmed that late-payment penalty clauses in telecom contracts may be declared unfair under the Unfair Terms Directive, even where national telecom rules impose no cap. Once a clause is found unfair, national courts must disapply it entirely rather than reduce the amount.

👀 Already on the calendar
On 14 October 2026, the General Court rules in Technius v Commission (T-134/24), on whether the Commission correctly calculated the average monthly active recipients behind a VLOP designation, and whether it may rely on third-party estimates rather than the platform’s own figures.

If you work in software consulting, you've probably heard it by now: AI is going to kill time & material.

I think it's true. And it's happening faster than most people expect.

For years we've sold software the same way. More people, more hours, bigger invoice.

But a small senior team with AI agents can now do work that used to take 20 people a year. Migrations, testing, legacy rewrites. That's exactly the work time & material was built on.

So what changes?

→ Clients will pay for outcomes, not hours. A small, sharp team charging more for less time will beat a big team billing by the day.
→ Engineers will split. People who just copy-paste requests into an AI become easy to replace. People who make the calls on architecture and quality become worth a lot more.
→ Vendors will earn less revenue but better margins. Middle layers with no real expertise will get squeezed out.
→ Buyers need to level up. If you can't judge a partner, or you won't share your real business goals with them, you'll get average results.

The smartest clients we work with are already doing this. Before they sign a big contract, they build a working version of the idea in MonstarX and put it in front of real users. By the time they talk scope, they know what's worth building.

One more thing. Cutting juniors because "AI can do it" is a mistake. Every senior was a junior once. Stop hiring them now and you won't have seniors in five years.

The partners worth keeping won't be the ones who say "yes, understood". They'll be the ones who ask hard questions and push back.

Is your business still running on time & material?
